Physical AI—systems that perceive, reason about, and act in the real world—is nearing a ChatGPT-like inflection point. BCG’s Japan-focused analysis argues that the winners will not simply buy robots; they will build data-driven learning loops that make deployed systems steadily better.

Japan’s labor shortage makes physical AI an urgent proving groundWith Japan facing an estimated 11 million-worker shortfall by 2040, physical AI could create $220 billion in annual value under BCG’s medium scenario by automating tasks and unlocking unmet demand.

Adoption depends on task capabilities, not broad industry labelsLogistics and repetitive manufacturing are advancing first because visual perception is improving. Construction and care remain harder: fine dexterity, reliable planning, and human-like touch still limit viable deployment.

The physical AI flywheel creates the durable advantageDeployed machines generate operational data, which improves models and accelerates further deployment. Companies should prioritize distinctive processes, since a sensor-rich machine can produce 1 terabyte of data per hour without guaranteeing useful learning.

Component makers and operators must act before standards and data advantages solidifyPrecision sensors, gears, computing, and software will shape the market, with key designs expected to settle by 2027–2028. Early deployments, human supervision, and disciplined data design can turn Japan’s domestic needs into globally scalable products.

Physical AI—AI that can understand and interact with the real world—has advanced rapidly, yet companies have been slow to build it into products or to buy and deploy it. That could change fast.Physical AI is set to follow the same nonlinear path as GenAI, which spent years in research before the launch of ChatGPT and other easy-to-use large language models rapidly shifted thinking. (See “What Is Physical AI?”)

What Is Physical AI?

The core of physical AI is a vision-language-action (VLA) model. It is the equivalent of an LLM, but it is trained on data about the physical world rather than mainly on text. This allows VLAs to turn a command such as “bring me that box” into a complex series of motor commands. In this report, we describe autonomous devices powered by physical AI as robots, but models like this have use far beyond C-3PO-style devices that look like a person.Physical AI can be embedded into a wide range of products, from earthmovers to highly sensitive medical devices. Today, many of these are controlled by a programmable logic controller, technology that has changed little since the 1970s. Replacing this with a VLA and the associated sensors may hardly change their appearance, but it represents a transformative upgrade.

We see one potential driver for this rapid acceleration in what BCG Institute calls the physical AI flywheel: initial deployment generates data, data improves capability, and better capability drives more deployment.Japan is likely to be an early adopter of physical AI. First, significant labor shortages, driven by a shrinking, aging population, create demand. Second, the capabilities that Japanese firms have developed over decades, such as precision component manufacture and manufacturing know-how, create an ideal starting position. Third, the Japanese government has devoted significant attention to the issue: the physical AI strategy announced in 2026 envisages $70 billion of public and private investment in physical AI before 2040, targeting 10 million AI-powered robots deployed across the country and a 30% share of the global AI-robotics market for Japanese companies.BCG Institute has developed three scenarios for physical AI deployment in Japan based on an analysis of technological progress and the demands of real-world occupations, with lessons for the rest of the world. In our “medium” scenario based on continued technology advances but no fresh breakthroughs, physical AI could generate around $220 billion a year of value in Japan by 2040. Our “maximum” scenario more than doubles that number. (See Exhibit 1.) The scenarios assume the highest possible adoption for each level of technological progress; real-world impact would likely be reduced by economic and social factors, such as environmental fit for automation, economic viability, regulatory preparedness, and public acceptance.

We see three opportunities for physical AI:Deploying robots in the real world. A five-level scale of capability helps map which tasks are next in line for physical AI—but organizations must also track environmental fit, economic viability, regulation, and social acceptance.Building physical AI into devices. We look closely at the opportunities for Japan’s world-leading components manufacturers and the question of cloud vs. on-device processing.Creating new business models or revenue streams. Any company collecting data in the real world should consider whether they have a physical AI opportunity.Across all these opportunities, the durable advantage is not created by simply buying or building. Instead, the advantage comes from compounding. This is the physical AI flywheel.The Physical AI Flywheel
The physical AI flywheel is the self-reinforcing cycle in which deployed machines generate data, data improves performance, and better performance drives wider deployment. (See Exhibit 2.)

The loop also connects the physical and virtual worlds: data from the physical world can improve digital simulation, and that improved simulation can improve real-world performance. This cycle is supported by an ecosystem in which sensor and component makers, AI companies, robot makers, and operating partners work together. These feedback mechanisms are apparent in highly demanding physical AI applications such as autonomous driving, where real-world mileage is augmented with repeated digital simulations of rare but high-danger scenarios, such as encountering a cyclist in fog. These, combined with over-the-air updates, create a fleet where performance is constantly improving.This continuous, data-based improvement cycle parallels Japan’s suriawase system (a system of integrated working within a company and between companies), which delivered high quality at low cost in sectors such as autos and precision manufacturing in the 1980s. Manufacturer and supplier engineers cooperated to create iterative adjustment processes. In the physical AI world, this becomes a continuous, run-time process of data collection and model improvement. The keiretsu relationships (longstanding corporate alliances) that powered this cooperation may help the digital version too; physical AI will learn faster if companies trust each other enough to share data up and down their supply chain.The physical AI flywheel can in some cases capture knowledge that is difficult to formalize. A skilled welder can judge a weld’s success by quickly assessing color, shape, and whether nearby metal has been distorted. A physical AI system can replicate and potentially improve on this judgment by collecting multiple images and linking them with subsequent observations of failure. But some judgments are still challenging: running a finger over a welded seam can find irregularities that are hard to see on camera, but in most settings today only human hands are sensitive enough to do this kind of test.

Using Physical AI: The Task-Specific Drivers
Our research into the value from physical AI reflects two mechanisms: reshaping work so people can be deployed to higher-value tasks and meeting demand that labor constraints would otherwise leave unserved. (See “Methodology: How BCG Estimated the Value Pool.”)

Methodology: How BCG Estimated the Value Pool

Our estimate measures the maximum economic value pool that physical AI could address across Japan’s labor market, before taking into account economic and social barriers. Such barriers could significantly decrease the actual value realized. The starting point is a bottom-up decomposition of all work in Japan: 20 industries, 232 occupations, and roughly 7,500 tasks within them, each mapped to the closest matching task in the US Department of Labor’s O*NET database of US job and worker characteristics. Yen were converted into dollars at the 2025 average of $1 to ¥150.For each task, we calculate a substitution rate, the share of that task’s work that physical AI could reshape or take over, which rolls up to two distinct value streams, both important.Cost saving is the value of physical labor directly displaced by physical AI. It is the number of workers times their wage times the substitution rate. Task substitution does not necessarily imply workforce elimination. The saved labor could shift to higher-value tasks or the many positions left unfilled amid Japan’s increasing labor shortage.New value is the additional revenue unlocked when lower costs or better service lets a company meet demand it previously had to turn away. The new value equals each industry’s profit margin times the substitution rate times a demand-scalability multiplier of up to 2x. This multiplier is not a simple estimate; it is set by whether there is real unmet demand, how price-sensitive the market is, and whether capital or other requirements limit how far output can scale.Cost saving is the primary driver of value. However, as physical AI is deployed more widely, new value becomes a larger proportion of the overall figure. (See the exhibit.)

These figures represent technical maximum potential, not a probable outcome: they assume every task that could technically be automated is automated. Other factors need to be considered to estimate actual adoption: environmental fit, economic viability, regulatory preparedness, and social acceptance. For applications in the home, health, or social care these are particularly important and may result in a wide gap between potential and real-world deployment. In addition, if physical AI can replace only a small fraction of the tasks within an occupation, a person may still be required for the remainder; the investment in automating that fraction alone may not be economically viable.Why the Three Scenarios Are Ten Times Apart
The three scenarios differ in how far physical AI’s capability frontier has advanced by the target year. Our analysis anchors this to a staircase of ten capability milestones, from basic object perception, through rigid grasping and multi-step task planning, up to outdoor perception and fine bimanual dexterity, with each milestone unlocking a specific class of occupation (stockers, then landscaping crews, then cooks, then construction laborers, then skilled trades such as carpentry). The underlying value curve is sharply backloaded.Restricted deployment analyzes the impact of physical AI based on the milestones physical AI has already reliably crossed today.Medium deployment assumes continued, incremental progress through the middle of that capability staircase, including stronger grasping, handling easily crushed objects, and early predictive maintenance-style capabilities, allowing deployment in occupations that are harder but not the hardest.Maximum deployment assumes the frontier reaches the final two milestones: reliable outdoor perception and fine bimanual dexterity, which unlock construction and the skilled trades.Because these final milestones are both the hardest to reach and by far the most valuable, together accounting for more than half of the total value at stake, reaching them, or not, is what swings the estimate by an order of magnitude, far more than any gradual improvement in between.

The third mechanism of value creation—creating innovative products and services that do not exist today—is addressed in our section on new business models later in the report.Japan’s challenging demographics drive both the reshaping of work and meeting labor demands that are underserved. Even with low economic growth, Japan could have a labor shortage of 11 million by 2040, according to Recruit Works Institute.So, where and when will this physical AI value arrive? At the industry level, the technology is already being adopted for logistics and repetitive manufacturing. We expect variable manufacturing and retail to follow over roughly the next two to five years. Full-scale diffusion in construction, households, hospitality, care, and materials is expected to take five to ten years or more. (See Exhibit 3.)

This industry-by-industry view hides the real drivers, which are more task-specific. At this level, the first set of drivers is the conditions at the site of deployment, as assessed across four dimensions: operating environment, economic rationality, regulation, and social acceptance.The second set of drivers is technological. Here, there are five levels of capability:Explicit Programming. This is the ability to execute motion sequences with high precision in a stable environment. It is a solved problem, but this function alone is not physical AI.Visual Perception. Amid strong progress, the economics of advanced visual perception are already becoming attractive. In some industrial applications, physical AI can eliminate some jigs, feeders, and manual adjustments that account for roughly 75% of conventional total cost of ownership and can reduce changeover re-engineering by up to half. Payback is centered on three to five years. Successful applications include the mixed palletizing robot arm built by Mujin, which can stack pallets of mixed-sized objects, ensuring maximum box count without exceeding a stipulated height.Dexterous Manipulation. Progress in dexterity has been less dramatic. Learned skills remain tightly coupled to specific tasks and hardware configurations, raising data and tuning costs. Although robot actuators can do many useful tasks, in most applications they lack the fingertip control that lets a human hand pick up a brick or an egg with equal ease.Workflow Planning. No fully reliable way exists for a robot to check that its plan will work except by trying it. Costly failures cannot always be caught before they happen, only responded to afterward.Planning and Reasoning. Here there are deeper constraints. Today’s physical AI models struggle to disentangle causal relationships. The result is the same failure pattern as workflow planning, but for a more fundamental reason: the model doesn’t understand cause and effect and therefore misunderstands the world it operates in.Within one industry, some tasks may require advanced perception, others will require high dexterity, and yet others may require advanced planning and reasoning. The adoption timetable is therefore not set at the industry level; it is set by the capability each process demands. For many manufacturing tasks, the missing capability has been visual perception; recent strong advances here are driving adoption.In contrast, many applications in domestic or care settings will require human-like levels of touch, so substantial progress is needed before adoption can be more widespread. It is the match between capability and task that drives whether deployment will meet ROI goals, not the industry. In some cases, companies can close the gap by redefining the task so today’s technologies are good enough.Another key issue is training data. Settings such as automated factories have a strong bank of data collected from current-generation robotics; there is no similar data set for, say, hotels or care facilities. Data from computer simulations can accelerate development, but it is most useful in static, low-contact tasks where digital simulations closely mimic real life; it is less useful in helping a physical AI model understand hard-to-model issues such as friction, deformation, and contact force—the interaction between a gripper and an object it is holding.In data-scarce environments, companies have options to kickstart the process:Deploy the sensing layer early. This means installing cameras, force sensors, and similar instrumentation into the environment before a physical AI model is ready, building data ready for deployment.Deploy with humans-in-the-loop. Here, operators remotely supervise or assist the system during early operation. This lets companies introduce and test equipment in the working environment, again building data ready for fully autonomous operation later.Choosing an option involves balancing factors such as the cost of errors and how quickly competitors could close the gap once a data advantage is established.Physical AI’s Value Is Not Limited to Labor Costs
Our analysis captures returns from physical AI that extend far beyond labor costs. For instance, a human-free factory may experience:More consistent quality, improving yield and customer satisfaction.Increased agility, allowing a faster response to demand.A move to 24-hour operation, increasing output.The model also captures the return from reducing the dependence on scarce expertise. This includes preserving the knowledge and experience of soon-to-retire workers, making expert-dependent work more reproducible across people and sites, and increasing process portability across domestic and overseas operations.Denso, one of Japan’s largest manufacturers, illustrates the ambition: it is starting a plant in 2028 in its Zenmyo facility west of Tokyo that aims for 24-hour unstaffed operation, with the knowledge and talent developed there deployed across sites in Japan and abroad. The strategic prize is not one highly automated factory, but a more flexible global production footprint.All companies that deploy physical AI, however, must understand that buying the technology is not the only challenge. Capturing its full value means redesigning operations, data foundations, workforce deployment, and decision rights. Hyundai shows the scale involved: it plans to deploy tens of thousands of robots in its factories, including Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid at its Metaplant America facility in Georgia, as part of a roughly $6 billion commitment to innovation and expanding strategic partnerships with US companies announced in 2025.Enabling Physical AI: Why Component Makers Must Shape the Standard by 2028
Physical AI is enabled by two layers: components that connect physical AI to the real world, and communications and edge computing that perform smart control. The competitive logic differs sharply.Components and the Physical Layer
For general components such as motors and power electronics, China holds a structural cost advantage supported by its deep component supplier network. The open opportunity is in areas that demand precision, reliability, and safety certification. These include highly precise gears and screws that deliver powerful but controlled movement, and advanced tactile sensors that tell the system how much force it is applying. Without them, a physical AI-powered device might lose its balance, miss its target, or crush what it handles.This is where Japanese suppliers have significant strengths. Moreover, the challenge of building these components means they represent an outsized part of the opportunity. One place where such components are concentrated is the robot’s “hand.” Morgan Stanley’s teardown of Tesla’s Optimus Gen 2 put the hands at around 17% of the total bill of materials.The market has yet to decide on which designs and specifications should be the reference building blocks. That creates a window to shape the standard, but it will soon close; we expect standard designs to begin solidifying in 2027–2028. The market for automotive electronic control units shows the value of steering a standard; suppliers such as Bosch, which helped shape the reference architecture, reinforced their leading positions and could bring compliant products to market fastest.For component makers, there are three routes to making their components the industry reference for physical AI products.Co-develop with robot and equipment makers before specifications and bills of materials get locked in place.Embed digital models of their components into simulation platforms such as Nvidia Isaac and Cosmos, so they become part of the design premise.Participate early in setting ISO and IEC safety standards to help shape the reference point for certification.Japanese suppliers such as Harmonic Drive Systems and Nabtesco have undoubted technical skills and hold leading global share in components such as precision reduction gears. But technical excellence alone is not enough. A sensor must produce data that the control layer can use and include software that calibrates output to real conditions. Increasingly, suppliers that can deliver hardware and software together will outcompete those that cannot. Suppliers that make this leap also have additional opportunities to influence standard-setting because standards increasingly define how hardware and software interact. This matters for Japan, which has often played catch-up in international rule-making despite the quality of its products.Edge Computing and the Intelligence Layer
The real world is complex and constantly changing. Any physical AI that aims to understand it needs substantial computing power, delivered fast enough to act on. The key question is where that computing happens.Localized Edge Computing. Physical AI is an important driver of a global edge computing market that IDC expects to grow to nearly $380 billion a year in 2028. Many companies building physical AI products may select a platform such as Nvidia’s IGX Thor platform, which has attracted a broad collection of hardware and software partners. These partnerships make it easier not only to build products, but to accelerate the path to important safety certifications, such as IEC 60601/62304 for medical devices and IEC 61508 for industrial equipment.Cloud-Based Processing. This can provide much more processing power, though it adds latency.Dynamic Switching. Potentially, the best of both worlds. Edge computing can be lightweight, energy-efficient, and used for reflexes such as stopping before a collision. Complex, multi-step reasoning or puzzling through ambiguous instructions can run on remote servers that could potentially power a fleet of devices. In 2026, SoftBank and Ericsson demonstrated a proof of concept that can dynamically offload local processing to nearby network servers based on the task’s complexity.For manufacturers, this is not just a technical choice. Wherever processing happens, the foundation models behind it are today developed largely in the United States and China. Sending data off-device adds security risks, and it also raises privacy issues for devices in health care or used in the home. If companies process data off-device, they should treat the choice of foundation-model ecosystem as a long-term business-risk decision, separate from components or connectivity. Fujitsu is working with Fanuc, Yaskawa Electric, and Kawasaki Heavy Industries on a sovereign collaborative control infrastructure to be used in industries such as manufacturing, retail, logistics and health care.In addition, Noetra, funded by Sony Group, SoftBank, NEC, Honda, and others, is developing foundation models for physical AI with government support, training on data from Japanese work sites and targeting advanced Japanese-language understanding.Advancing Physical AI with New Business Models
Physical AI will enable new products, services, and revenue models. Any company selling sensor-equipped hardware should ask three questions:What data does our product generate in the field?How can that data make the product smarter?And how can that improvement translate into revenue?However, the opportunity is much greater than smarter versions of existing products; physical AI will enable entirely new product categories, such as autonomous industrial robots, security robots, and those doing deliveries. In a scenario where every household has a robot, the resulting opportunity could rival or surpass today’s market for automotives and create a whole ecosystem with opportunities across component upgrades, AI models, data, and maintenance.These opportunities are not fully captured in our estimate of physical AI value creation, and that is by design. Our estimate quantifies value only from the user’s perspective: cost savings and demand expansion captured by companies deploying physical AI in their own operations. New products, services, and revenue models, where companies sell physical AI-enabled outcomes, data, or subscriptions to others, sit in a separate category.A Different Role for Integrators
Traditionally, integrators have generated value by carefully programming each robot’s movement and installing it on site. The VLA AI model installed in physical AI devices shrinks that effort considerably; robots will work out their own movement sequence based on the problem to be solved.Integrators in the physical AI world can instead generate value from managing installations on an ongoing basis. They can help accelerate the physical AI flywheel; data-driven improvements at one customer can be quickly rolled out to a large pool of others, creating value that any individual customer would struggle to replicate.In some cases, integrators may offer robots-as-a-service as a business model, with devices deployed for as long as customers need them and then moved elsewhere. This service may be used for proof of concept, to avoid capex, or workload peaks.Competitors will likely crowd in. These new players may include software providers, companies with expertise in specialized domains (such as health care), and new, venture-backed players. The venture-backed players may be scale players, whose playbook is to provide robots-as-a-service to highly fragmented industries where companies lack the capital or skills to buy and install their own equipment.Why Data Design Matters for Physical AI
The physical AI flywheel needs to be fed data with care. The physical world is an expensive place to repeat the data-lake mistake of collecting first and looking for uses later. Data must be sensed and processed, and much of it is noise. In a real-world environment with lots of events occurring at once, discerning cause from effect can be difficult. Experiments must also protect safety and uptime, and learning from one machine may need to be transferred to a fleet where hardware and software are highly mixed.These make data design critical. Companies must decide which data to capture and which decisions to improve. The alternative—collecting in bulk and then hoping to find some learning—is expensive when a single sensor-rich machine can generate a terabyte of data or more in an hour. Because each turn of the loop costs money, it should pass two tests: it must generate an economic return as the loop improves, and the data it captures should be sufficiently distinctive to drive differentiation. We call processes that pass both tests “differentiating processes.”How Can Companies Build a First-Mover Advantage in Physical AI?
Physical AI rewards first movers, but the advantage compounds slowly. Physical AI needs to sense the physical world for an extended period, unlike generative AI, which could immediately draw on the entire internet for training. Physical AI deployment needs capital, physical assets, integration, and data collection. Learning cycles take longer. (See Exhibit 4.)

Because of this, a “try everything” approach is not viable. Companies should:Create a shortlist of high-value opportunities.Map each against technology, maturity, and adoption conditions.Decide what to pursue now versus what to monitor and revisit later.Deciding how and when to build the physical AI flywheel must become part of the strategy.People are the custodians of that loop. Leaders must decide which work moves to AI, which higher-value tasks absorb freed capacity, who intervenes when AI misjudges, and how to capture skilled workers’ movements and judgment while they are still active. In some cases, data collection can begin before physical AI devices are ready for deployment.The most urgent task is to build loops around differentiating processes. A telltale sign is variation in tasks, operating environment, or the objects being handled. Processes that lack this—such as manipulating or inspecting items on a high-volume production line—may drive early value but offer limited opportunities to create durable differentiation.General-purpose robot foundation models are advancing fast and could narrow the gap with more specialized systems, as they have in other types of AI. Where leaders have already opened a gap, the advantage usually lies in proprietary data. This type of data can create competitive advantage even if the learning model becomes more commoditized.Two capabilities separate companies that compound data value from those that merely accumulate: a learning approach that captures signals of quality rather than volume and an upgradeable architecture that allows deployed systems to keep improving.Taking First Steps with Physical AI
Even where technology or adoption conditions are not yet ready, companies can begin collecting data and laying foundations. Leaders should:Start formulating the strategy. Begin with the future operating model, not today’s asset base. Ask: If physical AI were already available, what value would we deliver, and to whom? Then work backward to the differentiating processes, operating model, and roadmap.Seize the opportunity. Starting early builds a lead that buying the same robots later will not erase.Match activity to process maturity. If motion analysis can standardize work today, capture data now. If touch and sensory precision remain the constraint, record movement and judgment while skilled workers are active. If cross-process optimization is still beyond the technology, track maturity and time the start.Standardize procedures, quality standards, and exception handling. These are the entrances to the learning loop.Look for short-term wins. These help build momentum—and spin up the flywheel.Japan is likely to be a testbed market for many of these principles, but they apply globally. Global companies can use emerging lessons from Japan to see in close detail how the flywheel spins up, and how they can use it in their own operations. The transfer should run both ways. Japanese companies should consider whether partners abroad can help turn products built for the domestic market into global winners. These partnerships would also feed data back that can further spin the flywheel.More broadly, Japan can turn its most pressing domestic challenges, such as elderly care and automation of manufacturing sites, into product categories that overseas players want to enter while coordinating its own ecosystem so that individual companies do not lose collectively. Doing so requires guarding against Galapagos syndrome, in which products optimized for the home market fail to travel. Japanese companies should design for the conditions of overseas markets from the start, not adapt after the fact.The breakthrough moment for physical AI is approaching fast. Our projections show that buying physical AI may become commonplace; compounding advantage will not.The authors would like to thank Yoichi Hangai, Andrea Yang, Ziyi Wang, Kasumi Hatori, Yu Li, Mayu Matsumoto, Satoshi Matsuzawa, Yoshiki Kasuga, Erika Takeuchi, Jiawen Sun, and Nagi Cao for their valuable contributions to this report.
